<!-- mainthm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:A}
Let $\operatorname{Aut}_q(n):=\operatorname{Aut}\big(\operatorname{Cyc}(\langle q\rangle,\mathbb{Z}_n)\big)$, where $\operatorname{Cyc}(\langle q\rangle,\mathbb{Z}_n)$ is the cyclotomic association scheme of the subgroup $\langle q\rangle\le\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$ acting on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ by multiplication, defined in Section~\ref{sec:cyc}. Then,
\[
	\bigcap_{C} \operatorname{PAut}(C) \;=\; \operatorname{Aut}_q(n),
\]
where $C$ runs over all cyclic codes of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
<!-- end mainthm-1 -->
<!-- mainthm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:B}
Let $\operatorname{idx}_d(q):=\frac{\varphi(d)}{\operatorname{ord}_d(q)}$. Then, $\operatorname{Aut}_q(n)\ne\operatorname{Aff}_q(n)$ if and only if one of the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(E\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item\label{it:E1} $\operatorname{idx}_{n/p}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$ for some prime $p\ge5$ with $p\,\|\,n$.
\item\label{it:E2} $\operatorname{idx}_{n/p}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$ for some odd prime $p$ with $p^{2}\mid n$.
\item\label{it:E3} $\operatorname{idx}_{n/4}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$ and $8\mid n$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end mainthm-2 -->
<!-- mainthm-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:C}
Fix a prime power $q$. Then, the exceptional lengths $n$ for $q$ have density zero. In other words,
\[
\#\{n \in \mathbb{N}: n \leq x, \ \gcd(n,q)=1\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{Aut}_q(n)\neq\operatorname{Aff}_q(n)\}=o(x),
\]
as $x$ goes to infinity.
<!-- end mainthm-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:scheme}
Let $\Sigma$ be a color set, and $X$ a finite set. An \emph{association scheme} on $X$ over $\Sigma$ is a pair $\mathcal{C}=(X,\pi)$ with $\pi\colon X\times X\to\Sigma$ satisfying the following axioms:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(A\arabic*)},leftmargin=*]
\item\label{ax:surj} $\pi$ is surjective;
\item\label{ax:diag} $\pi(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$;
\item\label{ax:star} $\pi(y,x)=\pi(x,y)^*$ for all $x,y\in X$;
\item\label{ax:reg} for all $r,s,t\in\Sigma$ there is an integer $c^t_{rs}$ such that
\[
\#\{y\in X:\pi(x,y)=r,\ \pi(y,z)=s\}=c^t_{rs},
\qquad\text{whenever }\pi(x,z)=t.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Here $\Sigma(\mathcal{C}) := \Sigma$ is the \emph{color set of $\mathcal{C}$}, the integers $c^t_{rs}$ are the \emph{structure constants}, and $\operatorname{rk}(\mathcal{C}):=|\Sigma(\mathcal{C})|$ is the \emph{rank} of $\mathcal{C}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:schemealg}
Let $k$ be a commutative ring and $\mathcal{C}$ an association scheme over $\Sigma$. The \emph{scheme algebra} $k\mathcal{C}$ is the free $k$-module with basis $\Sigma$, with multiplication determined by
\[
s\cdot t := \sum_{u\in\Sigma}c^u_{st}\,u.
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:cyc}
The \emph{cyclotomic association scheme} of $K$ over $R$ is the pair $\operatorname{Cyc}(K,R):=(R,\pi)$ over the color set $R/K$, where
\[
\pi(x,y) := (y-x)K.
\]
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:cycscheme}
Let
\begin{gather*}
\operatorname{AGL}_1(R):=\{x\mapsto xa+b:\ a\in R^\times,\ b\in R\},\\
\operatorname{Aff}_K(R):=\{x\mapsto xk+b:\ k\in K,\ b\in R\}.
\end{gather*}
Then, $\operatorname{Aut}\big(\operatorname{Cyc}(K,R)\big)\cap\operatorname{AGL}_1(R)=\operatorname{Aff}_K(R)$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Consider a map $\sigma\colon x\mapsto xa+b$ with $a\in R^\times$ and $b\in R$. Then $\sigma y-\sigma x=(y-x)a$, so
\[
\pi(\sigma x,\sigma y)=(y-x)aK,
\]
and $\sigma$ preserves the coloring if and only if $(y-x)aK=(y-x)K$ for all $x$ and $y$. Taking $y-x=1$ shows that this forces $aK=K$, that is, $a\in K$; and conversely $aK=K$ gives $(y-x)aK=(y-x)K$ for every $x$ and $y$. Hence a map in $\operatorname{AGL}_1(R)$ preserves the coloring if and only if $a\in K$, which is the stated equality.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:cyccode}
A \emph{cyclic code} of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is an ideal of $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:spectrum}
For every cyclic code $C$ of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ there is a unique subset $J(C)\subseteq\Omega$ with $C\otimes F=\bigoplus_{a\in J(C)}F\chi_a$, and $J(C)$ is $\langle q\rangle$-invariant. The map $C\mapsto J(C)$ is an inclusion-preserving bijection from the cyclic codes of length $n$ onto the $\langle q\rangle$-invariant subsets of $\Omega$, with inclusion-preserving inverse.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:spectrum}
The set $J(C)$ is the \emph{spectrum} of $C$. For $T\in\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle$, the cyclic code with spectrum $T$ is denoted $M_T$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:count}
There are exactly $2^{|\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle|}$ cyclic codes of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, and the minimal ones are the $M_T$ for $T\in\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:idem}
Let $C$ be a cyclic code and let
\[
e_C:=\frac1n\sum_{a\in J(C)}\chi_a.
\]
Then, $e_C$ is an idempotent in $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$. Moreover, $C=e_C*\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$ and $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega=C\oplus C'$, where $C':=(\delta_0-e_C)*\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$ with $J(C')=\Omega\setminus J(C)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:sumspec}
If $C$ and $D$ are cyclic codes of length $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, then $C+D$ is a cyclic code with $J(C+D)=J(C)\cup J(D)$. In particular, $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega=\bigoplus_{T\in\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle}M_T$, and for each $T$, the code $M_T':=\sum_{T'\ne T}M_{T'}$ satisfies $M_T'=(\delta_0-e_{M_T})*\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$ and $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega=M_T\oplus M_T'$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:S}
Let $\mathcal{S}_q(n)$ be the set of all $f\in\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$ that are constant on each cyclotomic coset, or equivalently the set of all $f$ with $f(qi)=f(i)$ for every $i\in\Omega$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:S}
The set $\mathcal{S}_q(n)$ is the subalgebra of $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$ fixed by $\mu_q$, and
\[
\mathbb{F}_q\operatorname{Cyc}(\langle q\rangle,\mathbb{Z}_n)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \mathcal{S}_q(n),\qquad T\longmapsto\mathbf{1}_T,
\]
is an isomorphism of $\mathbb{F}_q$-algebras.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The identity $\mu_qf=f$ says $f(q^{-1}i)=f(i)$ for all $i$, that is, $f$ is constant on the orbits of $\langle q\rangle$. So $\mathcal{S}_q(n)$ is the fixed set of $\mu_q$, and it is a subalgebra of $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$ because $\mu_q$ acts as an algebra automorphism.

The colors of $\operatorname{Cyc}(\langle q\rangle,\mathbb{Z}_n)$ are the cyclotomic cosets. The scheme algebra $\mathbb{F}_q\operatorname{Cyc}(\langle q\rangle,\mathbb{Z}_n)$ defined in Definition~\ref{def:schemealg} is the free $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector space on the cyclotomic cosets, of dimension $\operatorname{rk}\big(\operatorname{Cyc}(\langle q\rangle,\mathbb{Z}_n)\big)$. The map $T\mapsto\mathbf{1}_T$ sends that basis to the indicators, which form a basis of $\mathcal{S}_q(n)$.

It remains to show that this vector space isomorphism is an algebra homomorphism. For every $T, T' \in \mathbb{Z}_n / \langle q\rangle$ and $i \in \mathbb{Z}_n$,
\[
(\mathbf{1}_T*\mathbf{1}_{T'})(i)=\#\{(u,v)\in T\times T':u+v=i\} = c^{\,i\langle q\rangle}_{TT'},
\]
where the second equality is obtained by applying Axiom~\ref{ax:reg} to the pair $(0,i)$, with $r = T$, $s = T'$ and $t = i\langle q\rangle$. Hence $\mathbf{1}_T*\mathbf{1}_{T'}=\sum_{T''}c^{T''}_{TT'}\mathbf{1}_{T''}$, which matches the multiplication rule of the scheme algebra.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:eCinS}
For every cyclic code $C$, $e_C\in\mathcal{S}_q(n)$. Moreover, the $e_{M_T}$'s for $T\in\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle$ are the primitive idempotents of $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$ and form a basis of $\mathcal{S}_q(n)$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
By~\ref{ch:mu}, $\mu_qe_C=\frac1n\sum_{a\in J(C)}\chi_{q^{-1}a}=e_C$, since $q^{-1}J(C)=J(C)$, hence $e_C\in\mathcal{S}_q(n)$ by Definition~\ref{def:S}. In particular, every $e_{M_T}$ lies in $\mathcal{S}_q(n)$. The $e_{M_T}$'s are pairwise orthogonal nonzero idempotents summing to $\delta_0$, hence linearly independent. Moreover, there are $|\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle|$ of them, which by Proposition~\ref{prop:S} is $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathcal{S}_q(n)$, so they form a basis of $\mathcal{S}_q(n)$. They are primitive because the $M_T$ are the minimal cyclic codes, by Corollary~\ref{cor:count}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:commute}
Let $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)$. Then, $\sigma \in \operatorname{Aut}_q(n)$ if and only if $\sigma(f*c)=f*\sigma(c)$ for all $f \in \mathcal{S}_q(n)$ and $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $f,c\in\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$. For $i\in\Omega$, evaluating at $\sigma i$, the function $\sigma(f*c)$ takes the value $\sum_jf(i-j)c(j)$, and $f*\sigma(c)$ takes the value $\sum_jf(\sigma i-j)c(\sigma^{-1}j) = \sum_jf(\sigma i-\sigma j)c(j)$. These agree for every $i$ and every $c$ if and only if
\begin{equation} \label{eq:comm}
f(\sigma i-\sigma j)=f(i-j)\qquad\text{for all }i,j\in\Omega.
\end{equation}

Suppose $\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}_q(n)$, and let $f\in\mathcal{S}_q(n)$. Then $f(i-j)$ depends only on the coset $(i-j)\langle q\rangle$, that is, on the color $\pi(j,i)$, which $\sigma$ preserves. So Eq.~\eqref{eq:comm} holds, and therefore $\sigma(f*c)=f*\sigma(c)$ for every $c$.

Conversely, suppose that $\sigma(f*c)=f*\sigma(c)$ for all $f\in\mathcal{S}_q(n)$ and $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$, so that Eq.~\eqref{eq:comm} holds for every $f\in\mathcal{S}_q(n)$. Taking $f=\mathbf{1}_T$ gives $\mathbf{1}_T(\sigma i-\sigma j)=\mathbf{1}_T(i-j)$ for every $T\in\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle$, that is, $(\sigma i-\sigma j)\langle q\rangle=(i-j)\langle q\rangle$. So $\sigma$ preserves every color and lies in $\operatorname{Aut}_q(n)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $\sigma\in \operatorname{Aut}_q(n)$ and let $C$ be a cyclic code, with idempotent generator $e_C\in\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:idem}, so that $e_C*e_C=e_C$ and $C=e_C*\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:eCinS}, $e_C\in\mathcal{S}_q(n)$. So Lemma~\ref{lem:commute} gives $\sigma(e_C*c)=e_C*\sigma(c)$ for every $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$. Since $\sigma$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$,
\[
\sigma C=\sigma\big(e_C*\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega\big)=e_C*\sigma\big(\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega\big)=e_C*\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega=C,
\]
hence $\sigma\in\operatorname{PAut}(C)$. This proves $\operatorname{Aut}_q(n)\le\bigcap_C\operatorname{PAut}(C)$.

Conversely, suppose that $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)$ fixes every minimal cyclic code, and fix $T\in\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle$. Then, both $M_T$ and $M_T':=\sum_{T'\ne T}M_{T'}$ are $\sigma$-invariant, the latter because $\sigma$ acts linearly. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sumspec} and Lemma~\ref{lem:idem}, $\mathbb{F}_q^\Omega=M_T\oplus M_T'$ and convolution by $e_{M_T}$ is the projection onto $M_T$ along $M_T'$.

Let $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^\Omega$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:idem} the idempotent of $M_T'$ is $e_{M_T'}=\delta_0-e_{M_T}$, hence $c=e_{M_T}*c+e_{M_T'}*c$. Applying $\sigma$ puts $\sigma(e_{M_T}*c)$ in $M_T$ and $\sigma(e_{M_T'}*c)$ in $M_T'$. Since convolution by $e_{M_T}$ is the identity on $M_T$ and annihilates $M_T'$,
\[
e_{M_T}*\sigma(c)=e_{M_T}*\big(\sigma (e_{M_T}*c) + \sigma (e_{M_T'}* c)\big)=\sigma\big(e_{M_T}*c\big).
\]
Thus, $\sigma$ commutes with convolution by each $e_{M_T}$. The condition is linear in the convolving element, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:eCinS} the $e_{M_T}$'s form a basis of $\mathcal{S}_q(n)$. So, $\sigma(f*c)=f*\sigma(c)$ for every $f\in\mathcal{S}_q(n)$ and every $c$, hence $\sigma\in \operatorname{Aut}_q(n)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:commute}. Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Aut}_q(n)\ \le\ \bigcap_C\operatorname{PAut}(C)\ \le\ \bigcap_{T\in\mathbb{Z}_n/\langle q\rangle}\operatorname{PAut}(M_T)\ \le\ \operatorname{Aut}_q(n),
\]
and the three groups coincide.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:EP}
Let $q$ be a prime power and $n\ge2$ with $\gcd(n,q)=1$. Then,
\[
\operatorname{Aut}_q(n)=\operatorname{Aff}_q(n)
\qquad\text{if and only if}\qquad
|\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)|\le2\ \text{ and }\ \Pr(n,q)\subseteq\{2,3\}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:idxmono}
Let $f$ be a divisor of $n$. Then, $K_{n,f}\subseteq\langle q\rangle$ if and only if $\operatorname{idx}_f(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
The reduction carries $\langle q\rangle$ onto the subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_f^\times$ generated by $q$, which has order $\operatorname{ord}_f(q)$, so $\langle q\rangle\cap K_{n,f}$ has order $\operatorname{ord}_n(q)/\operatorname{ord}_f(q)$. Dividing the order of $K_{n,f}$ by that order gives
\[
\big[K_{n,f}:\langle q\rangle\cap K_{n,f}\big]=\frac{\varphi(n)/\varphi(f)}{\operatorname{ord}_n(q)/\operatorname{ord}_f(q)}=\frac{\operatorname{idx}_n(q)}{\operatorname{idx}_f(q)},
\]
from which the result follows.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:stcrit}
Let $d\mid n$ and let $U=(n/d)\mathbb{Z}_n$ be the subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ of order $d$. Then, $U\le\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)$ if and only if $\operatorname{idx}_{n/d}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$ and every prime dividing $d$ also divides $n/d$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
We use the abbreviation $K:=K_{n,n/d}$ for simplicity. The coset $1+U$ consists of the $d$ residues congruent to $1$ modulo $n/d$, and $K$ consists of those of them that are units. So $K\subseteq1+U$, and the two coincide precisely when $|K|=d$. Here $|K|=\varphi(n)/\varphi(n/d)$, which equals $d$ times the product of $1-1/p$ over the primes $p$ dividing $n$ but not $n/d$. Therefore, $K=1+U$ if and only if every prime dividing $d$ also divides $n/d$.

We first prove the sufficiency. By Lemma~\ref{lem:idxmono}, $K\subseteq\langle q\rangle$, hence $1 + U = K \subseteq\langle q\rangle$. Since $U$ is an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}_n$, we have $\langle q\rangle\,U\subseteq U$, so $\langle q\rangle+U\subseteq\langle q\rangle(1+\langle q\rangle U)\subseteq\langle q\rangle(1+U)\subseteq\langle q\rangle$, and equality holds as both sides have the same size. Therefore, $U \le \operatorname{Tr}(n,q)$.

Assume conversely that $U\le\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)$. Taking the element $1\in\langle q\rangle$ in the identity $\langle q\rangle+u=\langle q\rangle$ gives $1+U\subseteq\langle q\rangle\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_n^\times$, so every member of $1+U$ is a unit. Therefore $K=1+U$, which implies that every prime dividing $d$ also divides $n/d$. Moreover, since $K$ lies inside $\langle q\rangle$, Lemma~\ref{lem:idxmono} gives $\operatorname{idx}_{n/d}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The result is trivial for $n = 1$, and we assume that $n \geq 2$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:EP}, $\operatorname{Aut}_q(n)\ne\operatorname{Aff}_q(n)$ if and only if either $\Pr(n,q)$ contains a prime $p\ge5$ or $|\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)|>2$. We show that the first is equivalent to Condition~\ref{it:E1}, and that the second holds if and only if Condition~\ref{it:E2} or Condition~\ref{it:E3} does.

Let $p\,\|\,n$. The Chinese remainder theorem gives $K_{n,n/p}=\mathbb{Z}_p^\times\times\{1\}$, so $p\in\Pr(n,q)$ if and only if $K_{n,n/p}\subseteq\langle q\rangle$, which by Lemma~\ref{lem:idxmono} says that $\operatorname{idx}_{n/p}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$. Restricting to $p\ge5$ identifies the fact that $\Pr(n,q)$ contains a prime $p\ge5$ with Condition~\ref{it:E1}.

Suppose now that Condition~\ref{it:E2} holds at the odd prime $p$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:stcrit} with $d = p$, we obtain a subgroup of order $p$ inside $\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)$, and $|\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)|\ge p>2$. Condition~\ref{it:E3} runs the same way with $d = 4$, for which Lemma~\ref{lem:stcrit} gives $|\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)|\ge 4>2$.

Conversely suppose $|\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)|>2$, and let $t:=|\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)|$. Being a subgroup of the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_n$, the group $\operatorname{Tr}(n,q)$ equals $(n/t)\mathbb{Z}_n$, and it contains $(n/d)\mathbb{Z}_n$ for every divisor $d$ of $t$. Let $d$ be an odd prime divisor of $t$ if one exists, and $d=4$ otherwise, which is available because a power of $2$ exceeding $2$ is divisible by $4$. Then, Lemma~\ref{lem:stcrit} gives the equality $\operatorname{idx}_{n/d}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$, and the fact that every prime dividing $d$ also divides $n/d$. If $d$ is an odd prime, the latter reads $d\mid n/d$, that is, $d^{2}\mid n$, which is Condition~\ref{it:E2}; and if $d=4$, it reads $2\mid n/4$, that is, $8\mid n$, which is Condition~\ref{it:E3}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:famA}
Let $p$ be a prime with $p\,\|\,n$ and let $m:=n/p$. Then,
\[
\operatorname{idx}_m(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)\iff \operatorname{ord}_p(q)=p-1\ \text{ and }\ \gcd\big(p-1,\ \operatorname{ord}_m(q)\big)=1 .
\]
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Since $p\,\|\,n$, we have $\varphi(n)=(p-1)\varphi(m)$, so the identity $\operatorname{idx}_m(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$ says that $\operatorname{ord}_n(q)=(p-1)\operatorname{ord}_m(q)$. The Chinese remainder theorem gives $\operatorname{ord}_n(q)=\operatorname{lcm}\big(\operatorname{ord}_p(q),\operatorname{ord}_m(q)\big)$. Writing $t:=\operatorname{ord}_p(q)$ and $u:=\operatorname{ord}_m(q)$, the identity $\operatorname{lcm}(t,u)=(p-1)u$ reads $t/\gcd(t,u)=p-1$, and since $t$ divides $p-1$ this holds if and only if $t=p-1$ and $\gcd(t,u)=1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:famA}
Take $q=2$ and $p=5$, where $2$ is a primitive root modulo $5$. For odd $k\ge3$, let $m:=2^{k}-1$. Note that $\operatorname{ord}_m(2)=k$ is odd and hence coprime to $p-1=4$, and $5\nmid m$, since $5\mid2^{k}-1$ would force $4\mid k$. Setting $n:=5m$, so that $5\,\|\,n$, Proposition~\ref{prop:famA} gives $\operatorname{idx}_m(2)=\operatorname{idx}_n(2)$, which is Condition~\ref{it:E1} at $p=5$. So by Theorem~\ref{thm:B} every $n=5\,(2^{k}-1)$ with odd $k\ge3$ is exceptional for $q=2$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:famB}
Let $p$ be an odd prime not dividing $q$ and suppose
\[
q^{\,\operatorname{ord}_p(q)}\not\equiv1\pmod{p^{2}}.
\]
Then, for $j \ge 1$,
\[
\operatorname{idx}_{p^{j}}(q)=\frac{p-1}{\operatorname{ord}_p(q)}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $t:=\operatorname{ord}_p(q)$. The hypothesis says that $q^{t}\ne1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{2}}^\times$, so the order of $q$ modulo $p^{2}$ is $pt$, and the standard description of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{j}}^\times$ for odd $p$ then gives $\operatorname{ord}_{p^{j}}(q)=p^{\,j-1}t$ for every $j\ge1$. Dividing $\varphi(p^{j})=p^{\,j-1}(p-1)$ by this order gives $\operatorname{idx}_{p^{j}}(q)=(p-1)/\operatorname{ord}_p(q)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:famB}
For $q=2$ the hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{prop:famB} holds at $p=3$, where $\operatorname{ord}_3(2)=2$ and $2^{2}=4\not\equiv1\pmod 9$; at $p=5$, where $\operatorname{ord}_5(2)=4$ and $2^{4}=16\not\equiv1\pmod{25}$; and at $p=7$, where $\operatorname{ord}_7(2)=3$ and $2^{3}=8\not\equiv1\pmod{49}$. For $n=p^{k}$ with $k\ge2$ the proposition gives $\operatorname{idx}_{n/p}(2)=\operatorname{idx}_n(2)$, which together with $p^{2}\mid n$ is Condition~\ref{it:E2}. So by Theorem~\ref{thm:B}, the lengths $3^{k}$, $5^{k}$ and $7^{k}$ with $k\ge2$ are all exceptional for $q=2$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:famC}
Let $q$ be an odd prime power, and let $e:=\operatorname{ord}_4(q)$ and $s:=s(q)$. Then, for $j \ge 2$,
\[
\operatorname{idx}_{2^{j}}(q)=\frac{2^{\,\min(j,\,s)-1}}{e}.
\]
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Since $2^{s}$ exactly divides $q^{e}-1$ and $s\ge2$, the integer $q^{e}+1$ is congruent to $2$ modulo $4$, and for $t\ge1$ the integer $q^{\,e2^{t}}+1$ is an odd square plus one, hence congruent to $2$ modulo $8$. Factoring
\[
q^{\,e2^{i}}-1=\big(q^{e}-1\big)\prod_{t=0}^{i-1}\big(q^{\,e2^{t}}+1\big)
\]
and adding the valuations therefore gives $v_2\big(q^{\,e2^{i}}-1\big)=s+i$ for every $i\ge0$. Now let $j\ge2$. The order $\operatorname{ord}_{2^{j}}(q)$ divides $\varphi(2^{j})=2^{\,j-1}$ and is a multiple of $e$, so it equals $e2^{i}$ for some $i\ge0$, and it is the least such value for which $2^{j}$ divides $q^{\,e2^{i}}-1$, that is, for which $j\le s+i$. Hence for $j\ge2$,
\[
\operatorname{ord}_{2^{j}}(q)=e\,2^{\max(0,\,j-s)}.
\]
Dividing $\varphi(2^{j})=2^{\,j-1}$ by this order gives $\operatorname{idx}_{2^{j}}(q)=2^{\,\min(j,\,s)-1}/e$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:famC}
For $n=2^{k}$ Conditions~\ref{it:E1} and~\ref{it:E2} are vacuous, so such a length is exceptional exactly when Condition~\ref{it:E3} holds, that is, when $k\ge3$ and $\operatorname{idx}_{2^{k-2}}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_{2^{k}}(q)$. For $k\ge4$ both exponents are at least $2$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:famC} turns that identity into $\min(k-2,s(q))=\min(k,s(q))$, which holds precisely when $k\ge s(q)+2$; and $k=3$ is excluded, since $\operatorname{idx}_{2}(q)=1$ while $\operatorname{idx}_{8}(q)=4/\operatorname{ord}_8(q)\ge2$ because $\mathbb{Z}_8^\times$ has exponent $2$. So $n=2^{k}$ is exceptional exactly when $k\ge s(q)+2$. Take $q=5$, so that $q\equiv1\pmod 4$ and $s(5)=v_2(4)=2$; then every $n=2^{k}$ with $k\ge4$ is exceptional for $q=5$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:prim}
For every $m\ge1$, the length $n=q^{m}-1$ is not exceptional for $q$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Suppose that $n=q^{m}-1$ is exceptional. Since $q^{m}\equiv1\pmod n$, and since $0<q^{k}-1<n$ whenever $1\le k<m$, we have $\operatorname{ord}_n(q)=m$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:B} one of the three conditions holds, and each of them has the form $\operatorname{idx}_{n/d}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$ for a divisor $d$ of $n$. Equivalently, $m = \lambda t$, where $t := \operatorname{ord}_{n/d}(q)$ and $\lambda := \frac{\varphi(n)}{\varphi(n/d)}$.

In Condition~\ref{it:E1}, $(d,\lambda)=(p,p-1)$ with $p\ge5$. In Condition~\ref{it:E2}, $(d,\lambda)=(p,p)$ with $p\ge3$. In Condition~\ref{it:E3}, $(d,\lambda)=(4,4)$. In all three cases, $\lambda \ge 3$ and $d \le \lambda + 1$. Since $\operatorname{ord}_{n/d}(q)=t$, the divisor $n/d$ divides $q^{t}-1$. Then,
\[
q^{\lambda t}-1=n\le d\,\big(q^{t}-1\big)<(\lambda+1)\,q^{t}-1.
\]
Adding $1$ and dividing by $q^{t}$ gives $2^{\lambda - 1} \leq q^{(\lambda - 1) t} < \lambda+1$. This is a contradiction, since $2^{\lambda-1}\ge\lambda+1$ for every $\lambda\ge3$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:densP}
The set $\mathcal{P}(q)$ has density $0$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:densQ}
The set $\mathcal{Q}(q)$ has density $0$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:orddens}
For every integer $r\ge2$, the set of primes $\ell$ with $r\mid\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$ has positive density in the set of primes.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:key}
Let $r\ge2$ be an integer. Then,
\[
\{n \in \mathbb{N}:\ n\ \text{has at most one prime factor}\ \ell\ \text{with}\ r\mid\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\}
\]
has density $0$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $L:=\{\ell\ \text{prime}:\ r\mid\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\}$, and let $\ell_1<\ell_2<\dots$ be its elements. By Theorem~\ref{thm:orddens}, the set $L$ has positive density in the set of primes, so $\#\{i:\ \ell_i\le t\}\gg t/\log t$, and partial summation gives $\sum_{i=1}^\infty 1/\ell_i=\infty$.

Consider $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and let
\[
P_k:=\prod_{i=1}^k\Big(1-\frac1{\ell_i}\Big),\qquad S_k:=\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{\ell_i}.
\]
Those $n$ divisible by none of the $\ell_i$ have density $P_k$, and for each $i$ those divisible by $\ell_i$ and by no other have density $P_k/(\ell_i-1)$. An integer with at most one prime factor in $L$ has at most one among $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k$, so the set in the lemma statement has upper density at most
\[
P_k\Big(1+\sum_{i\le k}\frac1{\ell_i-1}\Big) \leq e^{-S_k} (1 + 2 S_k).
\]
The result follows from taking the limit $k \to \infty$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathcal{P}(q)$, so that $\operatorname{idx}_{n/p}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$ for some prime $p\ge5$ with $p\,\|\,n$, and let $m:=n/p$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:famA}, we have $\gcd(p-1,\operatorname{ord}_m(q))=1$. Since $p-1$ is even, $\operatorname{ord}_m(q)$ is odd. For every prime $\ell\mid m$ the reduction $\mathbb{Z}_m^\times\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}_\ell^\times$ gives $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)\mid\operatorname{ord}_m(q)$, hence $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$ is odd as well. Therefore, $p$ is the only prime factor $\ell$ of $n$ with $2\mid\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:key} with $r=2$ gives the desired result.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:local}
Let $p$ be a prime, $a := v_p(n)$ and $m:=n/p^{a}$, and let $c$ be an integer with $1 \leq c < a$. If $\operatorname{ord}_n(q)=p^{c}\,\operatorname{ord}_{n/p^{c}}(q)$, then
\[
v_p\big(\operatorname{ord}_m(q)\big)\ \le\ a-1-c.
\]
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By the Chinese remainder theorem,
\[
\operatorname{ord}_n(q)=\operatorname{lcm}\big(\operatorname{ord}_{p^{a}}(q),\operatorname{ord}_m(q)\big),\quad
\operatorname{ord}_{n/p^{c}}(q)=\operatorname{lcm}\big(\operatorname{ord}_{p^{a-c}}(q),\operatorname{ord}_m(q)\big).
\]
Each $\operatorname{ord}_{p^{j}}(q)$ divides $\varphi(p^{j})=p^{j-1}(p-1)$ and has the same prime-to-$p$ part as $\operatorname{ord}_p(q)$, so the two orders above have equal prime-to-$p$ parts. Write $\alpha_j:=v_p(\operatorname{ord}_{p^{j}}(q))$ and $b:=v_p(\operatorname{ord}_m(q))$. Their $p$-parts are then $\max(\alpha_a,b)$ and $\max(\alpha_{a-c},b)$, so
\[
\max(\alpha_a,b)=\max(\alpha_{a-c},b)+c.
\]
The right-hand side exceeds $b$, so the left-hand side is $\alpha_a$, and then $\alpha_a\ge b+c$. Finally $\alpha_a\le a-1$, because $\operatorname{ord}_{p^{a}}(q)$ divides $p^{a-1}(p-1)$, so $b\le a-1-c$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $n\in\mathcal{Q}(q)$. By definition there is a prime $p$ for which either $p$ is odd with $p^{2}\mid n$ and $\operatorname{idx}_{n/p}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$, or $p=2$ with $8\mid n$ and $\operatorname{idx}_{n/4}(q)=\operatorname{idx}_n(q)$. Let $c:=1$ in the first case and $c:=2$ in the second, $a:=v_p(n)$ and $m:=n/p^{a}$. In both cases, every prime dividing $p^{c}$ divides $n/p^{c}$, so $\varphi(n)/\varphi(n/p^{c})=p^{c}$ and the index identity reads
\begin{equation} \label{eq:ord}
\operatorname{ord}_n(q)=p^{c}\,\operatorname{ord}_{n/p^{c}}(q).
\end{equation}
Moreover $c<a$ in both cases, since $p^{2}\mid n$ reads $2\le a$ in the first and $8\mid n$ reads $3\le a$ in the second.

For a prime $p$ and an integer $a \ge 2$, let $\mathcal{Q}_{(p, a)}(q)$ be the set of $n \in \mathcal{Q}(q)$ such that Eq.~\eqref{eq:ord} holds with $p$ satisfying $v_p(n)=a$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:local}, we have $v_p(\operatorname{ord}_m(q))\le a-1-c$, so $p^{\,a-c}\nmid\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$ for every prime $\ell\mid m$, since $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$ divides $\operatorname{ord}_m(q)$. Thus $p$ is the only prime factor $\ell$ of $n$ that can satisfy $p^{\,a-c}\mid\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:key} with $r=p^{\,a-c}$ shows that $\mathcal{Q}_{(p, a)}(q)$ has density $0$.

Let $y\ge2$, and let $\mathcal{Q}^{1}(q)$ be the subset of $\mathcal{Q}(q)$ consisting of those $n$ that are divisible by some $p^{a} > y$ with prime $p$ and $a\ge2$, and let $\mathcal{Q}^{0}(q) := \mathcal{Q}(q) \setminus \mathcal{Q}^{1}(q)$. Note that $\mathcal{Q}^0(q)$ is a subset of the finite union $\bigcup_{p^a \leq y} \mathcal{Q}_{(p, a)}(q)$, hence has density $0$. For $\mathcal{Q}^1(q)$,
\[
\#\{n \leq x : n \in \mathcal{Q}^{1}(q)\} \leq x\sum_{\substack{p^{a}>y\\ a\ge2}}\frac1{p^{a}} \ll \frac{x}{\sqrt{y}}.
\]
Therefore, $\mathcal{Q}(q)$ has upper density $\ll y^{-1/2}$. Since $y\ge2$ was arbitrary, that upper density is $0$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
